title: As an AI-native user, I can rely on faithful function/tool calling — typed tool definitions, parallel and multi-step calls — documented well enough to run an agent loop on this model
As a developer, I can get typed, structured outputs — JSON-schema-constrained responses or a natively typed answer format — so my code consumes model output without fragile parsing
As a developer, I can stream responses token by token (or get sub-second full answers) with the latency behavior documented
As a developer, every model's context window and token budgets are documented precisely — input/output limits per model, not marketing ranges
As a developer, I can send images, audio, or documents to the model — or the docs honestly scope the model to text-only input
As an ml-engineer, I can control how hard the model thinks — extended reasoning/thinking modes, effort levels, or confidence signals — through documented request parameters
As a founder, I can see public per-token prices for every current model without talking to sales
As a developer, I can read documented rate limits — requests and tokens per unit time, how tiers scale, and what a 429 looks like — before I hit them in production
As an ml-engineer, I can cut cost and latency on repeated context with documented prompt/prefix caching and its pricing
As an ml-engineer, I can submit asynchronous batch jobs at a documented discount versus real-time pricing
As a founder, I can set spending caps, budgets, or usage alerts so a runaway workload cannot generate an unbounded bill
As an ml-engineer, I can read a published model card or system card — capabilities, training approach, evaluation results, and intended use — for the current flagship model
As a developer, the vendor documents the model's failure modes and jagged edges — what it is bad at, in its own docs, not just what it aces
As an ml-engineer, published benchmark claims come with enough methodology — eval names, settings, harness or prompts — that I could reproduce or at least audit them
As a founder, the model shows up in independent third-party evaluations and leaderboards, so I am not relying only on vendor-run numbers
As a developer, I can pin an exact versioned model ID while aliases track the latest release, with the alias-to-version policy documented
As a developer, I can rely on a documented deprecation policy with advance notice and migration guidance before a model I depend on is retired
As an AI-native user, I can have an agent enumerate the live model catalog programmatically via a documented models endpoint
As a developer, model and API changes land in a maintained changelog or release notes I can follow
As an ml-engineer, I can download the model weights under a stated license and run them myself — or the platform is honest that weights are closed
As an ml-engineer, I can fine-tune the vendor's models on my own data through a documented self-serve path — hosted fine-tuning API or tunable open weights
As an AI-native user, a real derivative ecosystem exists around the model — community replicas, fine-tunes, or quantizations on public hubs — with clear attribution of what is and is not official
As a developer, I can sign up and mint an API key self-serve — no sales call, no waitlist gymnastics — and the docs say exactly how
As a developer, a quickstart takes me from zero to a first successful API call in minutes, with runnable code in my language
As a developer, official cookbooks or worked examples show real end-to-end tasks — not just single-call snippets — that I can adapt
As an AI-native user, I can point existing OpenAI-compatible tooling at the platform, or follow a documented migration/adapter path from other providers' SDKs
As a founder, the usage policy is clear about what I may build — prohibited uses, commercial terms, and data-handling commitments in plain language
As an ml-engineer, the vendor publishes safety evaluations or a responsible-release process for its frontier models — red-teaming, risk assessments, or a safety framework with teeth
As a developer, the platform gives me guardrail primitives — moderation endpoints, safety settings, or documented patterns for gating model output before it acts
As a founder, I can consume the same models through major clouds or gateways — Bedrock, Vertex, Azure, or OpenRouter-class routers — not only the vendor's own endpoint
As an AI-native user, I can plug the model into coding agents and agent frameworks through documented, official integrations — skills, plugins, or first-class SDK support
As an AI-native user, the community ecosystem around the model is genuinely alive — curated lists, third-party tools, routers, and integrations with active maintainers
